judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate File 418, which defines sex in state law as male or female based on a person's body at birth. It removes gender identity from the Iowa Civil Rights Act, so the act no longer bars discrimination on that basis in jobs, housing, public places and the other areas it covers. Birth certificates must record the sex assigned at birth, and the state may issue a new certificate only in the cases the act lists. It also reworded an existing ban on gender identity lessons in kindergarten through sixth grade to cover gender theory. The Iowa Senate passed it 33-15, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 856, which bars state agencies, local governments, universities and community colleges from spending any money on diversity, equity and inclusion offices, officers or programs. It defines those programs to include efforts to favor people by race, sex, color or ethnicity, and trainings on ideas such as unconscious bias or systemic oppression. Teaching, research, student groups, health services and legal compliance offices are not covered. Any person may report a violation to the attorney general, who may sue to stop it. The Iowa Senate passed it 34-16, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate File 615, which requires most adults on the Iowa Health and Wellness Plan, the state's Medicaid expansion, to work at least 80 hours a month to keep coverage. People under 19 or over 64, people with a disability or who are medically frail, parents of a child under six, high-risk pregnant women and people on unemployment benefits are exempt. The state must seek federal approval first. The act also lets a couple in the Medicaid program for working people with disabilities keep up to $21,000 in savings instead of $10,000. The Iowa Senate passed it 33-13, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2788, which adds rules for abortion drugs. Before any abortion, a doctor must examine the woman in person and screen for signs of coercion or abuse, and before prescribing abortion drugs must get her signed consent on the federal patient form. The drugs may be dispensed only in a health care setting, directly to the woman, except in a medical emergency. Anyone who dispenses them another way can be sued for damages, and providers who break the rules face license discipline. Miscarriage care and treatment of an ectopic pregnancy do not count as abortions, and an older fetal-heartbeat chapter that a newer chapter replaced is repealed. The Iowa House passed it 58-29, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 924, which lowers the minimum age for a permit to carry a handgun in Iowa from 21 to 18, and lets an 18-year-old get a permit to acquire a pistol or revolver. Federal law still bars licensed dealers from selling handguns to anyone under 21, and the act says a permit held by someone under 21 is not valid for a dealer sale, so those buyers must use private transfers. Before this act, only professional permits, for jobs such as security work, were open at 18. The Iowa Senate passed it 33-14, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2296, which bans cities and counties from issuing their own identification cards to residents. The only exceptions are ID cards for a government's own employees and elected officials, and the driver's licenses and state ID cards some county treasurers already issue on the state's behalf. Local community ID programs, which mainly served residents who could not get a state ID, end as a result. The Iowa Senate passed it 31-14, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate File 579, which stops cities and counties from passing civil rights laws that cover more kinds of discrimination than state law does. Cities of 29,000 or more no longer have to keep a local civil rights commission, which becomes optional. Complaints against a city or county go to the state civil rights office, and any party may move a complaint to the state if it sits unresolved for a year. The Iowa House passed it 60-26, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 2527, which shields farms, fuel makers, ethanol plants and other businesses from lawsuits over harm to the climate from their greenhouse gas emissions. A person suing must name each gas and prove, by clear and convincing evidence, that the harm came directly from the business breaking a specific emissions limit or permit. Without that proof, no court may award damages or any other relief. The Iowa House passed it 66-24, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 706, which raises the fines for officials who break Iowa's open meetings law. A member who takes part in a violation now pays $500 to $2,500, up from $100 to $500, and $5,000 to $12,500 for a knowing violation, up from $1,000 to $2,500. A court must now remove a member who has any prior violation, not only one that drew a fine. New officials must take a one-to-two-hour course on the open meetings and open records laws within 90 days. The act also makes two kinds of records confidential: legislative security camera footage and state employee key-card entry logs. The Iowa Senate passed it 34-13, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House File 299, which requires schools, child care centers and the state health department to tell parents about the legal exemptions from required vaccines whenever they communicate about immunizations. The exemption information must also appear on school and child care websites and in registration papers. The Iowa Senate passed it 32-16, and it became law.
